column2: EN
<align=left>The place hasn't changed. Feels different, though.</align>
<align=left>I travelled all this way and they had already had the funeral?</align>

<align=left>I hadn't been home for a long time before this. What I had learned on my return made me wonder if things had changed a lot in that time or if I had been too young to form a realistic picture of my family. </align>

<align=left>My mother was ill; very ill. I remember her being... absent as a child. Not distant; she had been a loving mother just one who was... different. </align>
<align=left>Only now I could see she had been dealing with something... significant. Father had been in a precarious place leading up to his death, which itself raised suspicions in me. </align>

<align=left>I resolved to stay in Marns for a time, to assist my mother. Not wishing to be a further drain on the family, I would go into the city and look for work. </align>
<align=left>All the while I would seek answers about my father's death. Something was not adding up and I wanted to know what. </align>
<align=left>It was time to go into the city.</align>
<align=left>I awoke in a cold sweat, loose memories of a dream chased away by the morning's light.  </align>

<align=left>My old room. It was... strange being back. I felt the same every time I returned home - though it hadn't really been my home since I was sent away, fourteen years prior. Just a place I came to see my family. Now just a place to visit my mother.</align>
<align=left>Where was the rest of this armour? I needed to ask Albrecht.</align>
<align=left>Why were these paintings off the wall? Albrecht would know.</align>
<align=left>Why did that child run?</align>
<align=left>...not supposed to see me?</align>
<align=left>If I lost sight of that child now, I'd never learn what he meant... </align>

<align=left>It was just as I remembered. Less cavernous, perhaps, but still an impressive room, with a grand staircase leading up to bedrooms and private offices. There was no sign of any of our servants, however. </align>
<align=left>And there beside the fire, my mother slumbered.</align>

<align=left>A dusty storeroom where my father kept momentos of his adventuring days. </align>
<align=left>This was another room I had been forbidden to enter, as a child.</align>

<align=left>Although I not yet succeeded in spreading pestilence within the city barracks, I was increasingly mindful that time was short.</align>
<align=left>My enemies were massing against me. To strike them with an unholy sickness would strengthen my hand. And yet, did I have time? Did I, indeed, wish to risk the entire populace by unleashing such a sickness?</align>
<align=left>I resolved to continue on my quest to infect the city guards.</align>
I decided to abandon the Plague of the Crypt, and press forwards with my studies.
<align=left>I would reconsider this decision the next morning.</align>
<align=left>Another day had passed. A day in which the city forces continued to strengthen.</align>
<align=left>My father's armour. It had been gathering dust here since the Lich War. </align>

<align=left>I could see that it had undergone several repairs, including a severe gash on the back - father had been lucky to survive that war. Then again, I considered anybody who came back from that war to be lucky. </align>
<align=left>I considered making use of it.</align>
<align=left>I left it where it was.</align>
<align=left>With some effort, I managed to leverage the breastplate and upper structure away from the lower parts, where it had been securely bolted.</align>
force the breastplate away from the main structure.

<align=left>I struggled with it for a time, but could not manage to separate the armour's component parts.</align>
<align=left>As I turned away, I smiled ruefully, pleased that my father was not witness to my impotent display.</align>
struggle with it.
<align=left>Though it was completely the wrong size for me to wear, I took it in case it might be of use.</align>
<align=left>It looked like there was something up there. I could probably reach it with a stretch. </align>

<align=left>A copy of the play 'Macbeth'.</align>
<align=left>Inside was an unaddressed letter my father had clearly intended to send but now never would.</align>
climb onto the shelf to reach it.
<align=left>I would consider coming back later...</align>
leave it where it is for now.
<align=left>There was nothing else up there but dust. Shoddy work that underlined Hoffmann's age.</align>
<align=left>After reading it, I put it in my bag.</align>
<align=left>My father's drink rack. Bottles of wine.</align>
<align=left>Nothing stronger in sight. </align>
<align=left>Surely he would have had some whisky in the house if he was so fond of it? But everything was wine, even his private stash was port - something didn't add up. </align>
<align=left>No whisky to be found. Was he really a whisky drinker at all?</align>

<align=left>This was clearly a trapdoor. Heavy-looking, reinforced with metal braces, and with no obvious locking mechanism. </align>
<align=left>I could not see any way to open it. Perhaps Albrecht might know something.</align>
<align=left>The trapdoor was currently open.</align>
<align=left>I left it that way.</align>
<align=left>With some effort, I swung it shut.</align>
<align=left>I heard the locking mechanism engage.</align>
<align=left>The trapdoor was currently closed.</align>
<align=left>I twisted the hexagonal bottle fully around.</align>
<align=left>Here was the tunnel's exit. Surely I was outside the city walls.</align>
<align=left>Although the trapdoor was locked and heavily reinforced, Albrecht had explained to me that an unusual wine bottle in the rack was the key.</align>
<align=left>After some searching, I found the unusual bottle that Albrecht had referred to. It had a hexagonal cross-section and sat in a tightly-fitting shelf of that same shape.</align>
<align=left>I carefully twisted the bottle.</align>
<align=left>I left it for now.</align>
<align=left>The heavy gears of some hidden mechanism echoed from below.</align>
<align=left>This was all that remained of the stairs up to the house. </align>
<align=left>The trapdoor above me was closed.</align>
<align=left>Quite a lot of straw was spread on the floor.</align>
<align=left>I noticed some curious markings peeking out from two or three spots where the straw was thin.</align>
notice something.
<align=left>Presumably there was a problem with dampness here.</align>
notice nothing.
<align=left>I cleared the straw.</align>
<align=left>I left it.</align>
<align=left>The ground beneath was bare earth.</align>
And inscribed faintly into it was the glyph I recognised from the Animate ritual!
<align=left>Some kind of arcane symbol had been traced into it.</align>
<align=left>A set of condolence cards was displayed on the table.</align>
<align=left>I opened the card from my uncle, baron Jervase.</align>
<align=left>I read the card from Guard Captain Willard Verner.</align>
<align=left>I checked the offering from a man named Lord Richard Carnell.</align>
<align=left>I read the card from my cousin, Lucus Van Elstrik.</align>
<align=left>I spotted a card from the queen of Rulsthen, Ulka III.</align>
<align=left>There was one from my friend Diedrik and his grandmother Sybil.</align>
<align=left>A second card from Diedrik was addressed to me alone.</align>
<align=left>One of the cards was enigmatically signed 'S.'</align>
<align=left>There was one from the local priest, Father Oliwier.</align>
<align=left>Pushed to the back was a card from my friend Sofia.</align>
I stepped away from the table.
<align=left>Ah, that's my one.</align>
<align=left>Yes, thank you Sofia. It means a lot.</align>

<align=left>A globe of the world. It even had the Americas on it. It was peppered with tiny red and black flags. I couldn't help but be curious as to what they meant but there was no sign of a key anywhere. </align>
<align=left>Amidst all the books on these shelves, an old volume entitled 'Séances For The Living' caught my eye.</align>
<align=left>I spent a while examining the books here but found nothing of interest for the moment.</align>
<align=left>I carefully pored though the pages in the old tome, and eventually found one which partially matched the key outlined in the Séances for the Living book.</align>

<align=left>It was the ritual entitled 'Séance', which I had already partially deciphered from Zend. </align>
<align=left>I could now understand the whole process.</align>

<align=left>I guessed that the page described in full a  mechanism for holding a séance with the deceased; certainly the text that I could now read as well as the illustrations suggested so.</align>
<align=left>I would need to decipher the rest of the page to be sure.</align>
<align=left>I took it in case it could be of use.</align>
<align=left>I could find it here again later if it seemed useful.</align>
As I searched the bookshelf, I recalled the strange book 'Séances for the Living' which I had found here earlier. I took it out and studied it again.
<align=left>It was an impressive collection of books with a wide range of titles. </align>
I could see a collection of the English poet Shakespeare, a copy of Machiavelli's The Prince and even some recent works such as Paradise Lost and a copy of Robinson Crusoe.
Most of it was lost on me, but I noticed Machiavelli's The Prince in the midst of it all.
<align=left>A surprising lack of military books, but then I guess he wanted away from all of that in his later years. </align>
<align=left>I didn't see anything here that looked as though it would help decipher the tome. </align>
<align=left>My father's desk. A pile of maps and writings scattered across it. It seemed he was as messy in later life as I recalled from my childhood.</align>
I examined the papers.
I looked at the maps.
I left it there, as messy as I found it. In truth I may have actually left it tidier.

<align=left>It was a scattering of personal and academic papers. My father was not, to my memory, a particularity learned man so I was surprised to see writings from Zosimos, Dee and Paracelsus. </align>

<align=left>After Albrecht mentioned the family affairs, I ignored the other texts and focused on a ledger showing my father's expenses. </align>
<align=left>Things were bleaker than I expected, and I could understand why Albrecht decided to cut back on the staff. With my father alive he could have held things together, certainly, but what were a butler and my mother to do with that loss of income?</align>

<align=left>A ledger also listed costs, income and expenses. I paid it little heed.</align>
<align=left>I could make out no discernable pattern in what my father had been researching. </align>
<align=left></align>

<align=left>Where had all his money gone? The ledger showed it bleeding out, but to where? </align>
<align=left>Perhaps in those books, he had been looking for a way to turn lead to gold? </align>

<align=left>There were also some letters on the desk. Of note, the one demanding payment 'or else' stood out. I was shocked to see my father was in debt to some shady sort, but given his finances I understood at least. </align>
<align=left>Up-to-date charts of the known world and sketchings of the local areas with various nearby tombs marked out. </align>
<align=left>Probably the sorts of things one considered for tactical planning. </align>
carry on examining the desk.
<align=left>None of it looked like it matched the writing in the tome, however. </align>
<align=left>One of the markings was in a small rocky canyon behind a chapel near the Dead Man's Gate. It was circled with 'Nightshade' written next to it.</align>
make a connection.
<align=left>One of the markings was in a small rocky canyon behind a chapel near the Dead Man's Gate. It was circled with 'Nightshade' written next to it.</align>
I searched for details on matters financial.
<align=left>What does it say, [name]?</align>
<align=left>Money problems, certainly. I will need to help around here.</align>
<align=left>Serious money problems I fear, and some kind of moneylender is involved.</align>
<align=left>Oh my!</align>
<align=left>I could make out no discernable pattern in what my father had been researching. </align>

<align=left>A portrait of Aldis Schmidt. I had a vague memory of the man from my youth. A general alongside my father and uncle; a close friend of theirs. It marked his death as 1726 - during the Lich War.</align>
<align=left>I recalled seeing a similar painting in the blacksmith's shop.</align>
<align=left>A bottle of port. Given my earlier findings, I would have expected whisky. Or a brandy, maybe. Perhaps he kept his stash elsewhere?</align>
<align=left>Surely he would have had some whisky in the house if he was so fond of it? But everything was wine - something didn't add up. </align>
<align=left>A bottle of port. Even his private stash didn't have whisky.</align>
<align=left>Some personal items of my father's.</align>
<align=left>There didn't seem to be much else of interest in the drawer. </align>
<align=left>No whisky to be found. Was he really a whisky drinker at all?</align>
<align=left>The drawer was locked. I needed to find the key.</align>
<align=left>Albrecht had cooked me up an almighty feast, but in truth, between the night before and the task ahead I had no appetite.</align>
<align=left>My possessions, such as they were. Some changes of clothes, some books. Nothing of real value. </align>
<align=left>My father wouldn't need it any longer so I decided to strap the family blade - my blade, now - to my waist. </align>
<align=left>A crate of my father's most precious wines. Why was this sitting in the entrance hall? </align>
<align=left>Even this, his most precious collection, had no whisky in it. That did not match the state he was found in - something was wrong here.</align>
<align=left>No whisky to be found. Was he really a whisky drinker at all?</align>
<align=left>I sat at the piano and played.</align>
<align=left>After a time, I ceased.</align>
<align=left>Sofia stood quietly and listened.</align>
<align=left>Alone, as I had played so many times as a child.</align>
<align=left>Father had many important meals at this table but I was never invited to those. </align>
<align=left>I recognised none of the people whose portraits hung on this wall, nor the names on the plaques. </align>
<align=left>The door to Albrecht's room was always locked. Understandable as it was his only place of refuge. </align>
<align=left>One of my favourite places in this house. Many was the night when Albrecht would bring me here to fix me a late snack once mother and father had gone to bed. </align>
<align=left>Where my cousin Lucus stayed when he was with us. I wondered when this room last saw use.</align>
<align=left>My father's study... Where he spent most of his time.</align>
<align=left>My parents' bedroom. Even now it felt like a violation to be here.</align>

<align=left>Two portraits of my mother. I recalled the more recent one being painted, when I was last home. The one of her as a younger woman must have been commissioned right around the time I was born, and it had always hung here.</align>
<align=left>Even in the older painting I could now see a hint of something in her face - despair perhaps - which I had never noticed before. </align>
<align=left>If father wasn't in his office he'd often be here. I used to wait for him to leave so I could look at whatever he had just been reading. </align>
<align=left>My mother's journal was a mess of disjointed sentences and lists, as if she was trying to remind herself of even the most basic of tasks.</align>
<align=left>An old party dress of my mother's. I remembered her wearing this at a big event in honour of Zelig when I was quite small.</align>
<align=left>I had fond memories of jumping into the sea from here, with my friends Diedrik and Flip. Long hot summers, a lifetime ago. </align>
<align=left>Our boat hadn't been tended to in an age. I wondered if it was still sea-worthy?</align>
<align=left>The storm had dragged our boat across the jetty. Here it lay, against the wall.</align>
<align=left>A fine carriage. Suitably comfortable for my journey here.</align>
<align=left>A mess of whisky bottles lay scattered on the ground beneath a battered bush. So this was where my father was found. </align>
<align=left>I didn't recall my father being a whisky drinker... </align>
recall something of your father.
<align=left>A shameful end to his life.  </align>
just feel disappointment.
<align=left>Then I spotted a small key, half buried in dirt. It must have fallen from my father's pocket when he was here. I put it in my bag.</align>
<align=left>Surely he would have had some whisky in the house if he was so fond of it? But all I had seen inside was wine and port. Something didn't add up.</align>
<align=left>On our doorstep lay the shelter of Marns Bay, and beyond that the majestic Adriatic.</align>
<align=left>The man nodded to me but said nothing.</align>

<align=left>I had no idea who had broken in, but before I could get too caught up in figuring it out, I needed to find a way to protect the house, should they come again. </align>
<align=left>I explained this to Albrecht, who only nodded solemnly in response. </align>
<align=left>Who do you think might be behind this? </align>
<align=left>Although... now I recall also that my father's financial ledger mentioned something about a debt, and it was marked with a strange sign.</align>
<align=left>I found an unsent letter from my father calling in a debt from a man named Oman. </align>
<align=left>Could it be the Shroud?</align>
<align=left>I could not but help think of the child Albrecht had hired to spy on me.</align>
<align=left>It's too early to say... We should continue to search.</align>
<align=left>It's too early to say but I'd wager it's linked to father's untimely demise. </align>
<align=left>Hard to say, I feel like nothing in this city is as it appears to be...</align>
<align=left>So you suspect foul play?</align>
<align=left>Perhaps, [Master], your father's recipe book has something in it that could be turned to protecting the house?</align>
<align=left>It was as if the strange book had heard my plea. Unsure what to do next I opened the tome. </align>
<align=left>Here has been rifled through, too?</align>
<align=left>I showed Albrecht the sigil I had copied.</align>
<align=left>My God, they even ransacked your mother's room. What were they looking for that they searched here? Jewellery? </align>
<align=left>They'd pulled all manner of books from the shelves. There seemed to be no order to the titles they had cast about. Perhaps they had to leave before they could finish?</align>
<align=left>Albrecht didn't sound convinced and neither was I. If all they wanted was jewellery then they'd have searched here and nowhere else.</align>
<align=left>This will take an age to reorder...</align>
<align=left>As Albrecht fretted, I scanned the books on the floor. The invaders had pulled out titles on the sciences, journals and books on esoterica I had not expected my father to own.</align>
<align=left>They did not seem to inspect them throughly - a quick skim and then discarded, moving onto the next. </align>
<align=left>Perhaps looking for letters or such hidden inside the tomes? Or hoping to find a lockbox disguised as a book?</align>

<align=left>A particularly strange book stood out. Its cover was made of tree bark and the pages within were rougher than normal. Whatever had been used to ink the pages was thick and amber coloured and shone like glass. It felt both old and primitive. </align>
<align=left>I took it, so that I could examine it more once this had all settled down.</align>

<align=left>As well as pulling books from the shelves they had clearly worked the shelves themselves in the hopes of finding a secret compartment. </align>
<align=left>From what I could tell they had had no luck with this.</align>

<align=left>I wished I had taken the time to order father's desk the day before. It was hard to tell if anything was missing, such was the mess here. </align>
<align=left>From what I could recall, though, everything was still here - if differently scattered. </align>
<align=left>I searched my belongings but could find no evidence that anything was missing. </align>
<align=left>It was hard to tell if this room had been searched or not for it was sparsely kept and there would be no evidence to have been left behind.  </align>

<align=left>I knew now what I needed to prepare the protection ritual. It appeared to be a relatively benign incantation which would protect our home.</align>
<align=left>The most difficult item would surely be the substance called Devil's Wood.</align>
<align=left>I informed Albrecht, then set him to the task of restoring order to the house while I found the required components.</align>

<align=left>I had been correct! The writing did match, though I still knew not the language I had found myself studying. </align>
<align=left>Nonetheless, I was now ready to have Grave Myst revealed to me. </align>
<align=left>I needed to find a way to decipher the rest of the page so I could prepare the ritual. </align>
<align=left>I wondered if there would be something in my father's collection -assuming it hadn't been taken in the burglary.</align>
<align=left>I couldn't be sure, but the markings on the Grave Myst page looked similar to those found in that strange rustic book I had just picked up from my father's office floor.</align>

<align=left>As if by magic, I found myself staring at a page titled Grave Myst. Though, I had not recalled seeing it before.</align>
<align=left>It was written in a few scripts and I could only decipher a few, enough to know it was a form of gas trap. Perfect, it seemed, to protect my home from further invasions.</align>
<align=left>Unsure what to do next I opened the tome. </align>

<align=left>I do. Father drank no whisky, only wine. By itself, easy to dismiss, as it could explain why he was found in such a state. </align>
<align=left>But that, combined with the rushed funeral and now this burglary? It is all too coincidental. </align>
<align=left>Gerhardht Oman? The harbourmaster? But what would he owe money to your father for? And why not just pay it, he's not a poor man. </align>

<align=left>Perhaps there is something unwholesome about the nature of the debt that Oman wanted erased?</align>
<align=left>The letter calling in the debt was unsent, perhaps that is what they sought when they searched our home?</align>
<align=left>I raised the issue with Oman and he was none too pleased. I'll have to find some other way to uncover this debt. </align>
<align=left>Whatever it is, I intend to find out. Though now, I might take a more indirect path in doing so. </align>
<align=left>Oh [Master] [Name], be careful. If he is involved in this burglary, who knows what else he might do to keep his secret - a secret he now knows you know - safe. </align>

<align=left>Yes, perhaps I overplayed my cards there. Let us hope that that is unrelated to this and he is just a harmless old man desperate to protect his reputation from some slight or other. </align>

<align=left>I suppose it could have been followers of the Lich? I find it hard to see them an organised group, more likely pockets of collaborators keeping their heads low. If a Shrouded One did this, I don't imagine it being anything more than a trophy hunt.</align>
<align=left>I found a letter demanding payment. It had this marking on it. </align>
That is, I believe, the mark of the Fishguard. Smugglers and racketeers. What would Master Zelig have to do with them?
<align=left>This I intend to learn. Where would I find them?</align>
<align=left>I confess I do not know, but given the nature of their organisation I'd wager the docks is a sensible place to start. </align>
<align=left>How convenient, then, that I have found myself working there. Perhaps one of my new colleagues will know something?</align>
<align=left>He said nothing but let out a low growl by way of agreement. </align>
<align=left>Albrecht, have you been paying a child to spy on me?</align>
<align=left>For a moment he said nothing.</align>

<align=left>Why no, of course not my [title]. You know me better than that.</align>
<align=left>A child, you say? Now why would they make up such a thing?</align>
<align=left>My [title]. We should conclude our investigation before you go about your business.</align>
<align=left>Ah yes, of course. I have met Ilona, the Fishwife. Lovely woman.</align>
<align=left>Can I help you, my [title]?</align>
<align=left>Outside, when I mentioned my father, you reacted strangely - is everything okay?</align>
<align=left>Tell me more of the funeral, Albrecht.</align>
<align=left>I saw my mother. She doesn't... She seems worse than normal?</align>

<align=left>His weight shifted. </align>
<align=left></align>
<align=left>Yes. I'm sure she will be fine in time [master] [name]. I'm... sure of it. </align>
I decided to bid him farewell and go on with my day.

<align=left>He paused a moment. </align>
<align=left></align>
<align=left>When I next saw Albrecht he was standing in the lobby beside my bags.</align>

<align=left>It has... already happened, my [title]. He was cremated and entombed yesterday. We did not receive word of your arrival so your uncle hastened the event as your mother's health has been understandably poor since his passing. I had hoped to allow you more time to rest after your trip before telling you.</align>
<align=left>I was shocked at this, and I am sure that Albrecht noticed. An uncharacteristic softness came over him, then.</align>
<align=left>It was a suitable affair, I assure you.</align>

<align=left>It was as you would expect. A grand event with a soldier's guard. Your uncle spoke, then the cremation. Once the ashes were gathered they were marched through town. The crypts were cleared and his remains were placed in the family vault. </align>
<align=left>If the gūl chased out are any indication, his ghost would have a suitable fight should God see fit to charge him so.</align>

<align=left>A hint of pride showed across his face, then. The most honourable burial possible. </align>
<align=left></align>
<align=left>Your uncle has commissioned a statue for the town's centre. Nasatia Masin has been hired for the task - and at no small cost.</align>
<align=left>The name meant nothing to me, but Albrecht seemed to feel her work was befitting my father's memory.</align>
<align=left>Why was the funeral so soon after his death? Surely they could have waited another day for me to arrive?</align>
<align=left>There was no word that you would arrive. And your uncle was worried that the Shroud would try to take the body. </align>
<align=left>The Shroud? I had thought that all worshippers of the Lich would have been taken care of by now, but clearly that was not the case. </align>
<align=left>Given your father's part in the war, his corpse would have made for a valuable trophy. </align>
<align=left>I'm surprised that the members haven't been chased down by now...</align>
<align=left>Do they have the ability to raise the dead? I thought that was lost with the Lich?</align>
<align=left>Why would anyone living pledge themselves to an undead sorcerer?</align>
<align=left>I have more questions about the Shroud. </align>
I had nothing else to ask about the Shroud.
<align=left>Albrecht, your letter didn't mention how my father died...</align>
<align=left>Your uncle has tried. But they are hard to find. They do not advertise themselves, you understand. </align>
<align=left>Then, what makes him so sure there are any left?</align>
<align=left>There were many mortals who fought on the Lich's side in the war. Not all were found. Your uncle believes that those who survived are out there. Waiting. </align>
<align=left>It is hoped so. The presumption is that they are waiting, hoping for a new death lord to rise. Taking the body would be more a gesture of resistance. </align>
<align=left>It is... hard to say. For some, this life isn't enough, I suppose. They want for more time. Or maybe they just want to see others suffer? But I speculate. </align>
<align=left>A sharp look from him then. He must not have wanted the question, but surely he expected it?</align>
<align=left>The herbalist, Haelan, performed the autopsy and said it was failure of the heart brought on by an overindulgence in liquor. </align>
<align=left>Why the herbalist? Why not a surgeon?</align>
<align=left>Drunk? In a bush?</align>
<align=left>Who found him?</align>
<align=left>I have more questions about my father's death. </align>
I could talk of my father's death no longer.
<align=left>I am afraid I do not know why. He is a learned man, I suppose?</align>
<align=left>Yes. Some broken bottles were found scattered around him. With the funeral, I've not had time to tidy the area, should you wish to look. It's around the back of the house.</align>
<align=left>The groundskeeper found him as he began his morning chores. </align>
<align=left>Anticipating my next question, Albrecht cut me off.</align>

Strength refers to physical power, and tasks such as arm wrestling or breaking things.
Agility refers to speed, agility and dexterity, and affects how fast you move in combat as well as how well you can complete physically awkward tasks.
Constitution refers to general health, stamina, and the ability to withstand poison, alcohol, or mental stress.
Acuity refers to logical thinking, and the ability to piece together clues to form a conclusion.
Knowledge refers to knowing important information such as local history, military or medical facts.
Investigate is the ability to notice important details or out-of-place elements. Also helps avoid ambushes.
Analyse is the ability to read other people's truthfulness and intentions.
Impress refers to your charm: getting people to like and trust you.
Convince is the ability to tell lies and talk people into doing your bidding.

The Verses of Sickness Date: 1723 Author: The Mage Jazani of Achaemenid (As translated and commented by Sir Ferdinand Obrenic) A Foreword: Greetings and Salutations! Introductions and explanations are in order before we get to the meat of this book. I am Sir Ferdinand Obrenic, explorer, linguist and vagabond extraordinaire! Among my travels within the strange and exotic lands of the Ottoman empire, I came across an old and forgotten temple littered with ancient Persian cuneiform. Among these inscriptions was a collection of chants and mantras attributed to ‘The Mage Jazani of Achaemenid’, of which he had collected during his travels within the Achaemenid Empire circa ~300 BC. The verses inscribed upon the walls centered mostly around ‘sickness’, ranging from simple, non-life threatening illnesses to what Mr. Jazani described as ‘dark possessions’. As follows are the least damaged and complete versions of the verses that I have translated to the best of my ability. Godspeed and safe travels! Signed, The Esteemed Sir Ferdinand Obrenic. The skies above they call for rain, Yet no answers shall they make When nearby fields lie those past slain Forbidden is the pond, must not partake For drinking of the dead and gone Slaking thirst to delay expiry By the river’s edge ‘tween the fronds Find oneself meeting the Almighty An interesting verse, speaking about the danger of corpses polluting nearby groundwater. Perhaps battlegrounds were so frequent around villages that they had to warn each other of such danger. O the dark spreads far O the dark spreads deep Between the walls and in the keeps A force which knows no keeper A force which knows no bounds Will hunt you like Duzakh’s hounds The burning fevers run The burning fevers rise O the dark will quicken your demise This passage seems to speak of a type of plague that spread within the Achaemenid Empire, perhaps a precursor to the plague which ran rampant across Europe hundreds of years later? Curious. The following verses were found in a room behind a crumbled wall. Perhaps a shrine to some sort of deity? Animal bones and ritualistic charms were littered around a well-used altar. The words were quite easy to translate; they flowed easily between the two languages, as if they yearned to be disseminated. This night I make a pledge Beyond the mortal plane A pact made amongst the dead sacrifice spilt from another’s vein. The spirits I shall guide In their unholy quest Unrestricted by earthly pride To do my bidding so possessed. Quite odd, but understandable that such a chant was hidden behind a wall in the temple. Dark magics and incantations were not the norm within Achaemenid society. Quite unheard of, actually. The dark, I call, to be spread Through my touch and from the dead A plague upon those who I choose Lament and pain their skin will ooze. Waiting below and in the crypt, Who shall next my spell afflict? Only when the next fast is broke, Will the pestilent spell then revoke. This last incantation seems to be referring to the plague that was mentioned earlier in the book, as if the reader were to actually cast the plague upon someone! It was then, after my last charcoal transfers of the cuneiform, the temple began to crumble down around me! Whatever old god lay in rest within that temple may have had enough of my poking and prodding. Any other mysteries or verses it may have held are now lost to time. I hope one day I have the chance to stumble across more of The Mage Jazani’s work in my further explorations of the land that was once known as the Achaemenid Empire. Your Esteemed Friend, Sir Ferdinand Obrenic

<u>From Fairest Creatures We Desire Increase</u>
From fairest creatures we desire increase,
That thereby beauty’s rose might never die,
But as the riper should by time decrease,
His tender heir mught bear his memeory:
But thou, contracted to thine own bright eyes,
Feed’st thy light’st flame with self-substantial fuel,
Making a famine where abundance lies,
Thyself thy foe, to thy sweet self too cruel.
Thou that art now the world’s fresh ornament
And only herald to the gaudy spring,
Within thine own bud buriest thy content
And, tender churl, makest waste in niggarding.
Pity the world, or else this glutton be,
To eat the world’s due, by the grave and thee.

<u>Then Let Not Winter’s Ragged Hand Deface</u>
Then let not winter’s ragged hand deface,
In thee thy summer, ere thou be distilled:
Make sweet some vial; treasure thou some place
With beauty’s treasure ere it be self-killed.
That use is not forbidden usury,
Which happies those that pay the willing loan;
That’s for thy self to breed another thee,
Or ten times happier, be it ten for one;
Ten times thy self were happier than thou art,
If ten of thine ten times refigured thee:
Then what could death do if thou shouldst depart,
Leaving thee living in posterity?
Be not self-willed, for thou art much too fair
To be death’s conquest and make worms thine heir.

<u>THE PUPPETSHOW</u>

The life of man to represent,
And turn it all to ridicule,
Wit did a puppetshow invent,
Where the chief actor is a fool.

The gods of old were logs of wood,
And worship was to puppets paid;
In antick dress the idol stood,
And priest and people bow'd the head.

No wonder then, if art began
The simple votaries to frame,
To shape in timber foolish man,
And consecrate the block to fame.

From hence poetick fancy learn'd
That trees might rise from human forms;
The body to a trunk be turn'd,
And branches issue from the arms.

Thus Daedalus and Ovid too,
That man's a blockhead, have confest:
Powel and Stretch the hint pursue;
Life is a farce, the world a jest.

The same great truth South Sea has prov'd
On that fam'd theatre, the alley;
Where thousands, by directors mov'd,
Are now sad monuments of folly.

What Momus was of old to Jove,
The same a Harlequin is now;
The former was buffoon above,
The latter as a Punch below.

This fleeting scene is but a stage,
Where various images appear;
In different parts of youth and age,
Alike the prince and peasant share.

Some draw our eyes by being great,
False pomp conceals mere wood within;
And legislators, rang'd in state,
Are oft but wisdom in machine.

A stock may chance to wear a crown,
And timber as a lord take place;
A statue may put on a frown,
And cheat us with a thinking face.

The Caged Creature of Cavazza
Date: Unknown
Author: Rocco di Zorzi

How I wish I had never accepted Lady Isabella Cavazza's invitation. How I wish I could return to the innocence of my former ignorance.

But now I have seen too much.

The fool that I am, I took her interest at the Doge's salon to be flirtation. At the time, I saw only a beautiful, powerful, alluring woman, unaware of the twisted thing lurking beneath that civilized surface.

Lured by lust and longing, I entered her estate and mistook the passion in her gaze for the lurid sort. But she did not lead me to her chambers as I had hoped, or to the balcony to converse. No. What she wished to show me was hidden. Deep in the dark.

Far below the elegant Cavazza estate, is a maze of stone and iron. At the very end of that maze was the prize she was so eager to share with me.

The thing shuffled its bare feet against the stone, meandering aimlessly in the dark. But as we grew near, it suddenly paused, like a cornered rat working up the courage to strike.

Isabella brought the torch close, and I saw… an abomination.

It was in the shape of a man, yet twisted. Long jagged claws and teeth dripping with rotten juices. Hunched with pallid grey skin, and cruel, cold, inhuman eyes, it flinched from the light, more at home in the dark. Thinking it only a sorry wretch, I took a curious step forward. It was then it leapt at me, a long arm reaching between the bars of its cell. The only reason my guts were not spilled across the floor in that moment, was that the Lady grabbed me by the collar and hauled me back.

'Gūl', she called it.

She told me that these gūli skulk about graveyards, caves, and on occasion, basements. As she looked adoringly at the freak, like a prized puppy, she told me how fond they are of stealing shiny things. She told me of the many and curious diseases they carry on tooth and claw, and how quick and ferocious they become by night.

Then she told me of the dead.

Of the corpses, both fresh and rotten, that the gūl craves. That they consume to sustain their unnatural existence as pitiable scavengers. Of how they seem to be at once alive and dead, inhabiting a terrible gulf between the two I had never known existed before that moment.

Of how she'd lost three men placing an iron collar upon this one. Of how she'd fed it their corpses and watched as it dug into their skin, their muscle, their fat, and even cracked open their bones to suck out the soft marrow inside.

When she turned to me at the end, I could see no difference between her eyes and the creature's. Both shone with a hunger as dark as it was insatiable.

In the shadows beneath that estate, I lost my faith. For what God would allow not just one such monster in His world, but two?

Memoirs While Studying the Ancient Cultures of the Adriatic
Date: 1652
Author: Roberta Van Obst, Royal Antiquarian to Edda I

My studies of the ancient material cultures of Rulsthen took a strange turn last winter. Even as my queen’s health has failed, her lust for knowledge of all kinds has risen, and she beseeched me to study what I could of the stone circles near Marns.

I was delighted to be stationed in this fine city over the winter; its pleasant climate was matched only by its most hospitable townsfolk. I enjoyed several evenings in the local drinking houses, talking to whomever would engage with me about the stones - their whereabouts, their history, and whatever else I could glean about them.

A number of alignments of standing stones are known in the region, but none more famous than the circle in the forest not far northwest of the main city gate. My friends of Marns spoke of buried artefacts there: bronze weapons, bracelets and pendants of amber, and numerous pottery urns filled with ash and mud. Some also whispered about some kind of ancient evil that lingered there amongst the stones.

Accompanied by a local farmer, Mr. Pavlovic, and with my retainer to defend me from wolves, we visited the site on a crisp December morning. I dug amongst the stones, finding at first only small shards of pottery. But then as I dug at the base of the central dolmen, a creeping fear began to descend on us all. A chill green fog rolled in from the sea, and I must admit that I did not complain too hard when Mr. Pavlovic insisted that we flee.

That evening we recounted our adventure over mugs of ale, and some local men insisted that we seek spiritual assistance before we returned to the site. Forthwith I visited the head priest, a Venetian cleric named Father Francesco Castelli, at the newly established and very fine cathedral at the centre of Marns. This good man agreed to accompany us to bless the site, that we might continue our work unmolested.

On our second and final visit we had scarcely begun to excavate before a howling wind whipped up and tore at us. Father Francesco brought out his holy water and commenced his spiritual work. A presence moved amongst us; it shrieked and gibbered and tossed the very earth all about. The brave man remained even as the rest of us withdrew. Eventually he too ran, driven away screaming as a lunatic. It was a week before the poor soul could even speak again.

The Greek Tale of Arachne Date: Unknown Author: Unknown In the ancient city of Colophon, there lived a gifted weaver named Arachne. Her skill with the loom was unparalleled, and her intricate tapestries told stories of wonder and beauty that captured the hearts of all who beheld them. Arachne's fame spread far and wide, drawing both admiration and envy. Becoming boastful, Arachne declared that her weaving skills were superior even to those of the goddess Athena, patron of crafts and weaving. Full of pride, Athena appeared before Arachne in disguise and warned her to show respect to the gods. But Arachne remained defiant. Athena revealed her true form, and a contest was set. Both Athena and Arachne wove their finest tapestries, and when their work was revealed, it was clear that Arachne's creation was a masterpiece of skill and creativity, surpassing even Athena's work. However, Arachne's subject matter mocked the gods in a most disprespectful way. Enraged by Arachne's audacity, Athena tore apart the tapestry and struck Arachne on the forehead with her shuttle. Overwhelmed by shame and despair, Arachne could not bear the weight of her humiliation. She took her own life by hanging. Athena was moved by the tragic fate of this talented mortal. With a mixture of pity and remorse, she transformed Arachne into a giant spider, that she might continue weaving but in a different form. And so, Arachne lived on as a spider, forever spinning intricate and magical rainbow-hued webs: at once a reminder of her once-great skill and of the consequences of mortals challenging the gods. A note was tucked into this book: Zelig: this is the book I referred to in our recent discussion. I am reminded of the colored webs that have been reported in the canyon beyond the southern gate. The key to the Plague ritual may lie therein, perhaps? A.S., 1724, December.

On the Conquest of Liches 
Date: 1729 
Author: Cecil Van Schuler

While Liches are by no means a new concept, until recently they could easily be dismissed as fanciful speculation or archaic myth. The recent war in Rulsthen, however, has forced us to jettison these false comforts. For the first time in contemporary history, a Lich operated in the open and it became impossible to disregard their existence. 

The Church has historically been reticent to encourage studies in this field; fearing that such pursuits might only bolster the heretical arts in question. But it is this author's assertion that if we wish to challenge such threats in the future, we must endeavor to understand their nature. 

Many reports describe Liches as non-living entities with the ability to create thralls out of the dead. However, unlike undead creatures in folklore, the Lich seems to retain full sentience. It does not act instinctively but, if the accounts from Rulsthen are to be believed, instead operates with intention, intelligence, and even malice. This allows a Lich to field armies and engage in broad military campaigns. 

Alarmingly, a Lich cannot be killed by conventional means and requires some form of extra-natural intervention.  

The threat posed by such a creature is apparent and immense. For this reason, we must secure sensible countermeasures, should another such being arise in the near future. 

The Van Elstriks, for all their heroism, have been disinclined to share the specifics of their triumph over the Lich in Rulsthen, and we must therefore turn to historical accounts and what limited contemporary sources exist. Unfortunately few, if any, of these scattered sources provide insight into the vulnerabilities of the Lich. We must then consider the less refined folk histories of the rural peasant population. 

Various tales allude to creatures with characteristics similar to the Lich. Both the Russian Koschei myths and the Baš Čelik stories of the southern Balkans involve entities that cannot be killed by bullet or blade, though the exact nature of their defeat remains variable. 

Could these tales have been inspired by Liches? Is there something to be gleaned in them about the nature and vulnerability of these seemingly deathless beings?

It would behoove us to study these tales and pry out some commonalities that could inform our future defense. Folk tales are, by their nature, malleable, inconcrete things, but if we apply a scientific approach to their study, it is this author's belief that we will find many details that persist across iterations. The source of our salvation might very well live within these particulars.

On The Safe Procurement of Devil's Wood
Date: 1726
Author: Cecil Van Schüler

As men of science, it is imperative that we strive to understand the world around us, even those quantities which might at first glance seem spurious or supernatural. For, as any true naturalist knows, our lack of understanding does not mean a lack of logic. We must simply unfurl the tangle of knowledge that lies before us.

I believe my very own inquiries into the phenomenon colloquially referred to as 'Devil's Wood' can provide an illustrative example of proper scientific inquiry.

I first heard of 'Devil's Wood' from a porter of mine, who had only recently arrived in the city and still carried the burdens of provincial ignorance. I ignored most of his superstitions outright, but there was something in the specificity with which he described 'Devil's Wood' that piqued my interest.

According to him, it was a tree that grew only in the darkest recesses of the forest, not unlike certain rare fungi, and its bark carried particular medicinal and alchemical properties. Despite its value, shavings from the tree were always in low supply. Often, the tree evidently resembled nothing more than a large and gnarled oak.

But at other times, he knew not when nor how, the plant transmorphed into something more novel, contorting its limbs and branches into strange, writhing patterns that my simple-minded porter described as tortured souls yearning to escape.

I, of course, understood these to be natural processes; perhaps some strange reaction to environmental conditions. I resolved to study this peculiar tree but my porter advised against it.

'Few men e'r return from such a hunt as that,' he warned me, in that plain language common to mountain folk. It seemed that there were myriad perils involved in scraping bark from the 'Devil's Wood,' and that many men died in the pursuit. The 'Devil's Wood,' he claimed, was a beacon to all manner of ghouls which congregated around it in the night. I was sure there was a rational explanation, but I was no fool.

Discovery is fraught with risk. I salute the intrepid explorers who journey into uncharted lands and contend with unknown quantities in their pursuit of enlightenment. But I chastise those who would undertake these risks when they are unnecessary, simply for the sake of adventure or individual renown.

The scientific mind is too valuable a commodity to chance haphazardly. For this reason, when we are presented with a challenge, it is our utmost duty to mitigate the risks involved, and where possible, use proxies of lesser scientific import. What is the loss of one or two laymen in the pursuit of knowledge that might help hundreds?

The porter, of course, refused to undertake the task himself, so I hired two woodsmen to enter the forest and locate one of these fabled trees. Neither returned.

I then sent another two men, instructing them to mark the tree, and the earth around it, with red paint. When they also failed to return, I sent a farm boy into the forest on a bright midday. He located the marked trees and stripped their bark in the safety of the early afternoon sun. But sadly, the wood proved useless. It exhibited no unique properties and remained inert throughout all my various experiments.

The porter told me this was because the bark has to be harvested in its more active state, when the souls bubble to the surface and turn the tree black. I sighed, knowing that these country superstitions always grow more elaborate when confronted with the cold truth of science.

Still, I sent three men into the forest and told them to fortify themselves around the tree before the afternoon mist rolled in from the sea. By evening, only one returned, bloodied and ranting.

In one hand he clutched a satchel of dark, contorted bark, and in the other, a small sapling that he assured me was 'Devil's Wood.' He raved about strange beasts and curious lights and I wondered if the tree also produced hallucinogenic qualities. I paid the man a bonus for his find, and gave the other men's widows an adequate recompense for their lost breadwinners.

The tree now sits in my upper study and indeed, at night or during foggy or misty days, the sapling turns dark and contorts in strange, mesmerizing patterns. It has caused an agitation among the neighborhood dogs and its bark does indeed exhibit novel properties when mixed with other agents, but the sapling refuses to grow.

Of course the porter tells me that it needs strange feed which is not so easy to find. 'Corpse Feed' he calls it. Thankfully, the supply of desperate men in need of coin is always plentiful...

Observations on the Ancient Egyptian Mummification Processes Date: 1725 Author: A. Schmidt. Abstract This treatise delves into the enigmatic practices of ancient Egyptian mummification, shedding light on their remarkable preservation methods. By examining historical sources, I have gained insights into how wood alcohol played a key role in preserving the deceased, ensuring their journey to the afterlife. I. The Significance of Mummification Ancient Egyptians considered mummification vital for the deceased's successful transition to the afterlife. Preserving the body was crucial, as it served as a vessel for the soul's journey beyond death. This belief gave rise to meticulous preservation procedures. II. The Mummification Process The mummification process encompassed several phases, with wood alcohol playing a pivotal role: Cleansing: To begin, the body underwent cleansing by immersion in a solution containing natron, a natural salt, and wood alcohol. This solution removed internal moisture and served as an antiseptic to inhibit decomposition. Evisceration: Organs, such as the liver, lungs, stomach, and intestines, were carefully removed and preserved separately in canopic jars. Each organ represented protection by a specific deity. Drying: After evisceration, the body underwent an extended drying process. Natron and wood alcohol were once again applied, both internally and externally, facilitating desiccation. The body often remained in a dedicated drying chamber for several weeks. Anointing: Once fully dried, the body received anointing with aromatic oils and resins. This step restored suppleness to the skin and imparted a pleasant fragrance to the mummy. Wrapping: The final stage involved wrapping the mummy in layers of linen bandages. This process could be intricate, with the inclusion of amulets and charms between layers, providing additional protection for the afterlife. III. Rituals and Prayers Throughout the mummification process, priests and attendants recited prayers and incantations, invoking the blessings of the gods to ensure the successful preservation of the deceased. Title: A Soldier's Account of The Battle of Marke Cross (Part 1)
Date: 1727
Author: Frederik Porter

Three weeks in the muck.

Three weeks of mud, and rock, and cold, and nothing but gruel to fill our stomachs. Three weeks of nervous, gut-wrenching waiting, each day bringing news of our lines collapsing further and further back.

Three terrible weeks, working to build a line of walls that none of us believed would halt their advance. Three weeks of festering resentment as we were told again and again that this is where we would halt them. This is where the winter stalemate would give us room to breathe. This is where the tide would turn.

None of us believed a word from those men on horseback, those men without even the smallest splash of mud on their bright, white trousers. We didn't believe them, but we kept digging, and lifting, and plastering just the same. We kept checking that our powder was dry, that our muskets were oiled, and that our blades were sharp. Because, even if we didn't believe a word they said, even if we knew our lives meant nothing to them, they sure as hell still meant something to us.

In our youth we'd been fed stories about the war with Venice, about brave young men from village hamlets who fought for their queen and received land as recompense. We heard songs of heroes and valor, and a proud kingdom standing against a tempest of Venetian steel.

And so, when this war started, when word of a force ravaging the east came our way, we joined. Only instead of heroics, we got muck. Instead of songs, we got slosh. And instead of Venetians ready to die on our bayonets, we got undead we couldn't kill.

And now, after months of beating a steady retreat, we waited for the decisive turn. Each night we collapsed into our trenches, our feet wet and cold, and our stomachs growling. And as we lay on our bedrolls, willing ourselves towards sleep, we heard the trumpeters call...

We rushed from our beds and to the battlements, loading our muskets with cold, agitated fingers that slipped against the metal. A handful of riders sprang into the open field before us. Each carried a torch as they galloped into the darkness and we watched those flickering lights recede into the distance, sending silent prayers that the men carrying them might reach their destination.

Then we heard the crack of muskets and two of the riders fell, their lights snuffed into the inky black. But another galloped onward and across the wide, open field. We could hear the clap of his horse's hooves against the earth, and then, again, the snap and burn of musket fire rang across the night.

The light wavered and dipped, but it did not disappear like the others. Instead it dangled close to earth, far too close for comfort. Its pace slowed to a trot, but it persisted. It persisted just long enough to reach its goal.

In an instant, the kindling we had set the day before burst into flames and spread across the field in either direction, painting the grassy earth in orange light. And in that light we saw them. A vast host of creatures that seemed almost human, but whose strange, stilted movements betrayed their unnatural construction.

Our cannons began to fire, splintering the enemy as they lumbered forward, until at last they came within range of our muskets. We unleashed one volley and then stepped back, allowing the next line to fire as we reloaded.

When we stepped forward again, we saw the effect of our barrage. To our surprise, it had proved effective, thinning the line of our enemies. We fired one more round, then another, until at last they were close enough to charge and our trumpets ordered us forward.

Title: A Soldier's Account of The Battle of Marke Cross (Part 2) Date: 1727 Author: Frederik Porter With the trumpets urging us onward, we poured over the battlement and rushed to meet our enemy. In truth, if we had lacked that surge of enthusiasm, the proximity of these creatures would have stupefied even the bravest among us. Their bodies were made of bloated, rotting flesh, the skin flayed in places where bullets had torn into them, and their faces were caked in mud and greasy, matted hair. They moved en masse, guided not by their eyes, but by some vision beyond the battlefield. Our blades slashed through their putrescent flesh, and our heavy hammers crushed their brittle, fractured skulls. If it had not been for the great quantity of them, we might have claimed an easy victory, but as it was, many of our number were swarmed and torn apart. Even Magnus. Dear Magnus, who as a child had caught fish with his bare hands, was not quick enough to escape their numbers. He parried one, avoided another, but a third slashed him across the belly and a pool of dark brown began to creep through his tunic. The ghoul moved to strike again, but a hammer smashed into its side, splintering bone and rending flesh. I ran to Magnus and caught him before he fell to the earth. Together we retreated across the field, away from the line of battle. He mumbled something in my ear about his dear sister, that I should not let her marry such-and-such merchant, but I could not focus on his words. Each time I looked back to the fighting, the battle seemed to be going somehow worse than before. The enemy numbers seemed never to change, and little by little, the quantity of our men dwindled. And then when I turned back to Magnus, I saw that he had stopped breathing. Exhausted, and without a comrade to carry, I dropped to the earth beside him. The sounds of battle lingered in the distance, carried by the gentle evening breeze, and I looked at my friend as he lay prostrate on the ground. I could not fathom that just a day before we had haggled for an extra portion of gruel, and laughed about the worthless trinkets we had traded away. And now he was dead, his open eyes staring into the sky above. I went to close the eyelids when something near the battle line drew my attention. A strange, robed figure moved through the fray. He was far away, but I could see that he wore no armour and brandished no blade. Only tattered fabric hugged his gaunt, skeletal frame and his face was as pale as the moon above. The eyes rested inside deep sockets, and even at this distance I could see that they carried no light. He seemed to hardly notice the bedlam around him until he lifted his hands. Then I understood why the battle was so beyond our reach... Around him, bodies began to rise from the mud. Their movements were stilted and uneven, but our men, so recently cut down, could not be mistaken. They lurched forward and began to grab and tear at their former comrades. It was mesmerizing in its horror, and through it all the figure moved as calmly as if he were on a Sunday stroll, a wave of bodies rising and falling around him. And then I heard a rustling beside me. The body that had been Magnus raised itself out of the muck in a series of unnatural contortions. Bones crunched against one another as the arms splayed outwards, sinew snapped, and blood, useless blood, oozed from the gaping wound at its stomach. I readied my bayonet but could not strike. Not until I studied that face for something, anything, familiar. I looked at the stubble on the chin, remembering that Magnus had complained about his inability to shave at the front. I looked at the nose, still crooked from where he'd broken it as a child, and then I looked at the eyes. It was the eyes that saved me. Those dead, empty eyes, looking at nothing in particular, eerily detached from the movement of the body. They betrayed the fact that Magnus was gone, that this creature had simply usurped his vessel. I struck forward, burying my blade inside its chest and heaving the creature away from me, though for a moment I thought I could register a look of anguish in its macabre expression. Unable to keep fighting, I clambered up and ran, leaving the battle behind, letting the sounds grow faint, either by distance or because the fight was well and truly lost. I do not know how long I ran, but in due course I collapsed against a large oak. When I was awoken the next morning, I was surprised to find a patrol of soldiers standing around me. Wasting no time, they informed me that the battle had been won, that the great enemy host had been defeated, but I could not imagine how. No earthly power could have saved us from that onslaught. What, then, was the source of our salvation?

The Final Dance
Date: 1520
Author:  Boris Vostenum

A young man came to Marns; his eyes wild, his clothing absent. His body was caked in mud. He collapsed right there in the market square. Taking pity on him, my wife implored me to carry the poor wretch home so that she might tend to him. We cleaned him and lay him to bed.

For three days and nights the man thrashed and sweated, though he did not wake. He roared and screamed. Few of his words made sense, but through it all he kept shouting the name Vila. Vila Samodiva. Why had she tempted him so, and why had she left him in the end? Could they not have one last dance?

On the fourth day the man awoke, though a strange malady remained on him. He refused all food and water, and would speak only of the beautiful Vila. How her ravishing looks and her beautiful singing were all he desired. How the memory of her enticing dance was all the sustenance he required. Her long blonde hair.. her bright blue eyes.. her gown of moonbeams and her hair adorned with wild flowers.

Alas, but the man continued to refuse all food and water, despite my wife’s pleading. He would only say he wanted nothing but to be back with Vila, and since she had left him he had no desire to live. We called Father Albert, and the good man performed an exorcism. All was in vain though, and on the seventh day the poor man died.

<size=150%>Kubla Khan</size>
<size=120%>By Samuel Taylor Coleridge, 1816</size>

In Xanadu did Kubla Khan
A stately pleasure-dome decree:
Where Alph, the sacred river, ran
Through caverns measureless to man
   Down to a sunless sea.
   
So twice five miles of fertile ground
With walls and towers were girdled round;
And there were gardens bright with sinuous rills,
Where blossomed many an incense-bearing tree;
And here were forests ancient as the hills,
Enfolding sunny spots of greenery.

 But oh! that deep romantic chasm which slanted
Down the green hill athwart a cedarn cover!
A savage place! as holy and enchanted
As e'er beneath a waning moon was haunted
By woman wailing for her demon-lover!

And from this chasm, with ceaseless turmoil seething,
As if this earth in fast thick pants were breathing,
A mighty fountain momently was forced:
Amid whose swift half-intermitted burst
Huge fragments vaulted like rebounding hail,
Or chaffy grain beneath the thresher's flail:

And mid these dancing rocks at once and ever
It flung up momently the sacred river.
Five miles meandering with a mazy motion
Through wood and dale the sacred river ran,
Then reached the caverns measureless to man,
And sank in tumult to a lifeless ocean;
And 'mid this tumult Kubla heard from far
Ancestral voices prophesying war!

   The shadow of the dome of pleasure
   Floated midway on the waves;
   Where was heard the mingled measure
   From the fountain and the caves.
It was a miracle of rare device,
A sunny pleasure-dome with caves of ice!

   A damsel with a dulcimer
   In a vision once I saw:
   It was an Abyssinian maid
   And on her dulcimer she played,
   Singing of Mount Abora.
   Could I revive within me
   Her symphony and song,
   To such a deep delight 'twould win me,

That with music loud and long,
I would build that dome in air,
That sunny dome! those caves of ice!
And all who heard should see them there,
And all should cry, Beware! Beware!
His flashing eyes, his floating hair!
Weave a circle round him thrice,
And close your eyes with holy dread
For he on honey-dew hath fed,
And drunk the milk of Paradise.

<size=150%>The World Is Too Much with Us</size>
<size=120%>By William Wordsworth, 1802</size>

The world is too much with us; late and soon,
Getting and spending, we lay waste our powers;—
Little we see in Nature that is ours;
We have given our hearts away, a sordid boon!

This Sea that bares her bosom to the moon;
The winds that will be howling at all hours,
And are up-gathered now like sleeping flowers;
For this, for everything, we are out of tune;

It moves us not. Great God! I’d rather be
A Pagan suckled in a creed outworn;
So might I, standing on this pleasant lea,

Have glimpses that would make me less forlorn;
Have sight of Proteus rising from the sea;
Or hear old Triton blow his wreathed horn.

<size=150%>Darkness</size>
<size=120%>By Lord Byron, 1816</size>

I had a dream, which was not all a dream.
The bright sun was extinguish'd, and the stars
Did wander darkling in the eternal space,
Rayless, and pathless, and the icy earth
Swung blind and blackening in the moonless air;

Morn came and went—and came, and brought no day,
And men forgot their passions in the dread
Of this their desolation; and all hearts
Were chill'd into a selfish prayer for light:

And they did live by watchfires—and the thrones,
The palaces of crowned kings—the huts,
The habitations of all things which dwell,
Were burnt for beacons; cities were consum'd,
And men were gather'd round their blazing homes
To look once more into each other's face;

Happy were those who dwelt within the eye
Of the volcanos, and their mountain-torch:
A fearful hope was all the world contain'd;
Forests were set on fire—but hour by hour
They fell and faded—and the crackling trunks
Extinguish'd with a crash—and all was black.

The brows of men by the despairing light
Wore an unearthly aspect, as by fits
The flashes fell upon them; some lay down
And hid their eyes and wept; and some did rest
Their chins upon their clenched hands, and smil'd;

And others hurried to and fro, and fed
Their funeral piles with fuel, and look'd up
With mad disquietude on the dull sky,
The pall of a past world; and then again
With curses cast them down upon the dust,
And gnash'd their teeth and howl'd: the wild birds shriek'd
And, terrified, did flutter on the ground,
And flap their useless wings; the wildest brutes
Came tame and tremulous; and vipers crawl'd
And twin'd themselves among the multitude,
Hissing, but stingless—they were slain for food.

And War, which for a moment was no more,
Did glut himself again: a meal was bought
With blood, and each sate sullenly apart
Gorging himself in gloom: no love was left;

All earth was but one thought—and that was death
Immediate and inglorious; and the pang
Of famine fed upon all entrails—men
Died, and their bones were tombless as their flesh;

The meagre by the meagre were devour'd,
Even dogs assail'd their masters, all save one,
And he was faithful to a corse, and kept
The birds and beasts and famish'd men at bay,
Till hunger clung them, or the dropping dead
Lur'd their lank jaws; himself sought out no food,
But with a piteous and perpetual moan,
And a quick desolate cry, licking the hand
Which answer'd not with a caress—he died.

The crowd was famish'd by degrees; but two
Of an enormous city did survive,
And they were enemies: they met beside
The dying embers of an altar-place
Where had been heap'd a mass of holy things
For an unholy usage; they rak'd up,
And shivering scrap'd with their cold skeleton hands
The feeble ashes, and their feeble breath
Blew for a little life, and made a flame
Which was a mockery; then they lifted up
Their eyes as it grew lighter, and beheld
Each other's aspects—saw, and shriek'd, and died—

Even of their mutual hideousness they died,
Unknowing who he was upon whose brow
Famine had written Fiend. The world was void,
The populous and the powerful was a lump,
Seasonless, herbless, treeless, manless, lifeless—
A lump of death—a chaos of hard clay.

The rivers, lakes and ocean all stood still,
And nothing stirr'd within their silent depths;
Ships sailorless lay rotting on the sea,
And their masts fell down piecemeal: as they dropp'd
They slept on the abyss without a surge—
The waves were dead; the tides were in their grave,
The moon, their mistress, had expir'd before;
The winds were wither'd in the stagnant air,
And the clouds perish'd; Darkness had no need
Of aid from them—She was the Universe.
